subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that ∫₀^(π/2) x/(sinx + cosx) dx = π/(2√2) log(√2 + 1).

mark_split.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
Add to reach an x-free integral
Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)

insider_note: The whole question reduces to the helper integral ∫₀^(π/2) dx/(sinx+cosx), which also appears when ∫₀^(π/2) sin²x/(cosx+sinx) dx is worked. A student who reaches it should recognise the form instead of re-deriving it from scratch.

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Only the x in front changes; the denominator sinx + cosx is symmetric, so it stays the same.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2 − x) + cos(π/2 − x) = cosx + sinx = sinx + cosx — the denominator is symmetric, so it never changes under this property.
steps.why: The denominator sinx + cosx is symmetric under the swap sinx ↔ cosx, so it is unchanged by x → π/2 − x; only the numerator's x becomes π/2 − x, which is what makes the addition step work.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to change x to π/2 − x in the numerator as well as inside sin and cos.
Writing sin(π/2 − x) + cos(π/2 − x) as sinx − cosx instead of cosx + sinx.

steps.label: Add to reach an x-free integral
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. x + (π/2 − x) = π/2 is what cancels the x term.
steps.memory_tip: x + (π/2 − x) always cancels to a plain π/2 — the same cancellation trick used throughout this chapter.
steps.why: Adding the two equal forms cancels x and (π/2 − x) down to a plain π/2, leaving the x-free integral ∫₀^(π/2) dx/(sinx + cosx).
common_mistakes: Adding the numerators incorrectly and not getting the constant π/2.
Losing the factor of 1/2 when isolating I from 2I.

steps.label: Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the R sin(x+α) rewrite and the cosecant integral.
steps.memory_tip: sinx + cosx = √2 sin(x + π/4). Dividing by it turns the integrand into a cosecant.
steps.why: The R sin(x+α) rewrite turns 1/(sinx + cosx) into (1/√2)cosec(x + π/4), so the integral becomes a cosecant integral carrying the constant π/(4√2) built from the π/4 that came out of the numerator.
common_mistakes: Missing the π/4 factor carried down from the addition step, so the constant in front is wrong.
Forgetting the 1/√2 factors inside the sine sum.

steps.label: Evaluate the log limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. This is exactly the answer the question asks to show — underline it.
steps.memory_tip: tan(3π/8) = √2 + 1 and tan(π/8) = √2 − 1, and their ratio is (√2 + 1)².
steps.why: Rationalising the fraction inside the log gives a perfect square, and log(a²) = 2 log(a) cancels the outer factor of 2 with the 4 in the denominator, leaving exactly the result the question asks to show.
common_mistakes: Not rationalising (√2+1)/(√2−1) before taking the log.
Arriving at a value that is off from the printed result by a factor of 2 — a sign that the log(a²) = 2log(a) step was skipped.
